content.title: About
content.content: Brisket is a large cut of beef taken from the front chest area of the animal. The meat is richly flavored, moderately fatty, and has a characteristic fibrous texture, making it ideal for low‑and‑slow cooking and smoking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brisket is a staple in classic American barbecue, especially Texas‑style smoked brisket.
When cooked properly, the muscle fibers break down, creating a tender, “pull‑apart” texture.
The cut is known by different names worldwide: in Russia it’s called “грудинка”, in Japan “ブリスケット”.
Brisket is high in collagen, which turns into gelatin during long cooking, enhancing juiciness.
Traditional Texas smoking can take 12 + hours at low temperature.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Brisket provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Good source of iron
items.content: Red meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals contribute to immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Collagen
items.content: Slow cooking releases collagen that becomes gelatin, beneficial for joints and skin.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Brisket contains a notable amount of saturated fat, so it should be eaten in moderation, especially by those with cardiovascular concerns.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor pathogens such as E. coli; cook to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Brisket is rich in purines, which can exacerbate gout symptoms in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Brisket is typically prepared by slow roasting, smoking, braising, or simmering. Before cooking it is often rubbed with a dry spice blend (salt, pepper, paprika, garlic). After cooking, slice against the grain. It can be served as sliced meat, used in sandwiches, salads, or as a base for stews.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh brisket in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw in the refrigerator before cooking, never at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate candy are small sweets made from chocolate (milk, dark or white) with a variety of fillings such as nuts, caramel, fruit, spices, and more. They have a rich cocoa flavor, aromatic notes, and are often coated with glaze or sprinkles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first chocolate bar was created in 1847 in England.
Chocolate candies are popular gifts for holidays like Valentine’s Day, Easter, and Christmas.
Dark chocolate contains over 70% cocoa and is considered healthier than milk chocolate.
In some countries (e.g., Switzerland) per‑capita consumption exceeds 10 kg per year.
Chocolate candies can be gluten‑free, but always check the filling ingredients.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Dark chocolate is high in flavonoids, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Mood‑enhancing
items.content: Chocolate stimulates serotonin and endorphin production, improving mood.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Chocolate provides magnesium, iron, zinc, and copper, important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains some fiber
items.content: When nuts or dried fruit are included, they add dietary fiber.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Sugar and fat deliver fast energy, useful during periods of high activity.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive intake can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Candies often contain nuts, milk, soy lecithin – common allergens.

items.title: Caffeine and theobromine
items.content: Large amounts may cause insomnia or rapid heartbeat, especially in children.

items.title: Trans fats in some varieties
items.content: Certain industrial candies use hydrogenated fats, which are harmful to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Candies can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, added to baked goods, ice cream, or dessert sauces. For a softer taste, they are sometimes gently warmed to melt the chocolate.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep candies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Above 20 °C the chocolate may melt, and high humidity can cause a white bloom (fat bloom).

livers-chicken-chopped-with-eggs-and-oni.title: Chicken Liver, Chopped, with Eggs and Onion

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken liver is a nutrient‑dense organ meat rich in iron, B‑vitamins, and high‑quality protein. In this dish the liver is finely chopped and simmered with eggs and onion, resulting in a tender, flavorful, and nourishing meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken liver contains more vitamin A than beef liver.
Cooking liver with onion helps mellow its natural bitterness.
Eggs add lecithin and vitamin D, boosting the dish’s nutritional profile.
Liver is quickly absorbed and is often recommended for anemia.
The combination is a classic in Russian cuisine, known as liver sauté or pâté.

items.title: Rich source of iron
items.content: Heme iron from liver is highly bioavailable and supports normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Provides B12, riboflavin, and niacin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Protein from liver and eggs aids tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Vitamin A and antioxidants
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Egg lecithin
items.content: Lecithin promotes liver function and helps fat metabolism.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: Both liver and eggs are cholesterol‑rich; people with hypercholesterolemia should limit portions.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked liver may harbor bacteria; ensure it is cooked through.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to eggs should avoid this dish.

items.title: Excess vitamin A
items.content: Large amounts of liver can lead to hypervitaminosis A.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a main course with potatoes, rice, or vegetables. It can also be used as a filling for pies or spread as a pâté on bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. It freezes well for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Cinnamon Waffle (3090) is a crisp, sweet waffle flavored with ground cinnamon. It is made from wheat flour, eggs, milk, butter, and natural spices, giving it a warm, spicy aroma and a golden crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cinnamon used in the waffle contains antioxidants and may help boost metabolism.
Traditional Belgian waffles are often served with cinnamon, but in this product the spice is incorporated into the batter.
Waffles store well: they stay crunchy for up to 7 days in a sealed package.
Cinnamon waffle is popular in colder months as a comforting dessert.
The sweet waffle and spicy cinnamon combo makes it suitable for breakfast or a snack.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Cinnamon is rich in polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Cinnamon may aid digestion and help regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The waffle provides a quick source of carbohydrates, useful for replenishing energy after activity.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The batter supplies vitamins B1, B2, and B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The waffle contains calcium and iron, supporting bone health and blood formation.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The waffle contains wheat flour, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet waffles can be calorie‑dense; those monitoring blood sugar should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Cinnamon in large amounts
items.content: Excessive cinnamon may irritate the stomach; it is advisable not to exceed the recommended serving size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cinnamon waffle can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, served with yogurt, ice cream, fresh berries, or drizzled with honey. For a softer texture, lightly toast it.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the waffle in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator to maintain its crispness.
